card.title: Leaf
card.summary: Portfolio project for the Google UX Design Certificate. Full UX process with a real usability study (SUS 76).

hero.title: Leaf
hero.tagline: Care for your plants without guessing when to water them.

problem.heading: A visual and functional language for daily care.
problem.body: Leaf was born as the capstone for my Google UX Design Certificate: an app that helps indoor-plant owners organize watering, light, and general-care reminders. The challenge wasn't technical — it was finding the right tone: useful without being controlling, calm without being boring.

research.heading: I started by listening.
research.body: I designed personas, ran a competitive audit, defined the value proposition, and framed 'How Might We…' questions and goal statements. Research surfaced two common failure modes across the category: asking users for too much upfront, or turning plant care into an anxious to-do list. Leaf had to do the opposite.
bullets: Personas grounded in real user interviews.
Competitive audit across 5 apps in the category.
Prioritized value proposition and 'How Might We…' questions.
Goal statements to scope the MVP.

process.heading: From wireframes to a design system.
process.body: I designed low-fidelity wireframes first, iterating on feedback before touching color or typography. The design system (palette, typography, components) grew as a reusable library — every ReminderCard, button, and bottom-sheet overlay lives as a component in Figma. The app was prototyped in high fidelity and moved to production with Claude Code via MCP.
flows: Home — next care at a glance

results.heading: Real usability study.
results.body: I ran a study with 5 participants using the System Usability Scale (SUS). The final score was 76 — above the industry average (68), in the 'good' range. What mattered more than the number was what the study surfaced.
learnings: Users wanted to see at a glance which plant needed attention today — I redesigned the home to prioritize 'next care' over full inventory.
Onboarding asked for too much upfront — I broke it into progressive steps with an option to defer detail.
Reminder copy worked better concise and warm-toned, not like a system notification.

reflection.heading: What I take away.
reflection.body: A good design system isn't about having many components — it's about having the right ones and using them consistently. And user research doesn't stop when design starts; it comes back to you on every iteration. If I started over, I'd invest more time in the usability study and less in polishing mockups before testing them.
